en: The Great and Vast Jewel-Pavilion Well-Situated Secret Dhāraṇī Sūtra,
Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Tang Dynasty.
Translated by Imperial Decree. Chapter One: The Introduction. Thus have I heard.
At one time the Buddha was staying in the great city of Rājagṛha;
at the time of his first assembly, he had subdued ten billion (*koṭi*) demonic armies.
And having subdued all non-Buddhists,
he abandoned birth and death and crossed over the various torrents.
At that time, hundreds of thousands of nayutas of *gaṅgā-rūpin-brahma* māra-armies pervaded the world.
At that time, by the Buddha’s supernatural power,
the World-Honored One transformed this great earth so that it became entirely composed of vajra,
ensuring that the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa would not hear of any fear.
At that time, the various weapons rained down by Māra’s army were all transformed into flowers in the four-way intersections of Rājagṛha city.
Spontaneously, lotus flowers emerged from the earth;
each flower had a thousand petals and was adorned with the seven treasures.
With a pedestal of gold and a stem of lapis lazuli, they rose as high as the Brahma Heaven.
Various kinds of light radiated, pervading the ten directions.
From within those flowers, a voice spontaneously issued forth,
reciting a dhāraṇī named "Excellent Awakening."
The mantra is as follows:

Namo daśadig-tathāgatānām. (1) Oṃ maṇi (2) vajrī (3) ratnaye (4) vajrī (5) maraseṇi (6) vidyārājñi (7) hana hana (8) vajrarājñe (9) tarapaya tarapaya (10) sarva-mara (11) prabodhani (12) hūṃ saṭṭāra saṭṭāra (13) buddhame ’tiṣṭha (14) sarvatathāgata (15) vajrakalpa (16) dhiṣṭhihi (17) svāhā. (18) At that time, within that lotus...
Having finished reciting the mantra,
he again uttered a sublime sound that pervaded the trichiliocosm, saying:
"Excellent, Tathāgata Śākyamuni!"
Having already crossed the great ocean of birth and death,
he has utterly destroyed the armies of Māra and departed from the dust of afflictions;
having shattered the shell of ignorance, he has kindled the great torch of the Dharma.
By the majestic power of this dhāraṇī,
this great earth was transformed into vajra, subduing the armies of Māra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi...
Filled with joy and leaping for gladness, the hair on his body stood on end.
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, from which Buddha did this vidyā-mantra first originate?"
"I have never before heard or seen such a thing.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi:
"There is a dhāraṇī named 'The Great and Vast Jewel Pavilion, the Secret of Excellent Abiding.'"
By his majestic power, he was able to transform this realm of three thousand great thousandfold worlds into vajra,
and all the weapons of the entire host of Māras were transformed into lotus flowers.
By the majestic spiritual power of that dhāraṇī, the hosts of Māras were subdued,
and lotuses sprang up in the crossroads.
Had it not been for the majestic power of that dhāraṇī, he would not have attained perfect enlightenment.
I have been unable to subdue the hosts of tens of millions of Māras,
nor have I been able to dry up the great ocean of afflictions and kindle the great torch of the Dharma throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kotis of kalpas.
Although he practiced difficult and arduous austerities,
he was still unable to achieve the fruit of bodhi;
it was only upon hearing that dhāraṇī at that time that he finally attained perfect enlightenment.
That dhāraṇī possesses great power and great excellence; it is the true Dharma.
It accomplishes the Dharmakāya of all Tathāgatas and is capable of invoking the names of those mantras.
This constitutes having already invoked the names of all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, of the ten directions;
if one can read, recite, receive, and uphold [this],
it constitutes making offerings to and prostrating before all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, of the ten directions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi made offerings to the Buddha with various kinds of flowers, incense, unguents, and powdered incense.
Having completed these offerings, he circumambulated the Buddha three times to the right.
Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, this dhāraṇī possesses great majestic power and great excellence.
We pray only that the World-Honored One will, for the sake of all sentient beings throughout the world, [bestow it upon them]."
One should not benefit others through inferior dharmas;
rather, one should benefit them with superior dharmas.
Why is this? Because this dhāraṇī is the true body of the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Sentient beings are inferior and do not apply themselves with diligence;
they are beset by many delusions and distractions, and are ignorant, dull-witted, and obtuse."
Attached to various sensual desires, they lack faith in the True Dharma;
they do not respect their father, they do not respect their mother,
they do not respect śramaṇas, they do not respect brāhmaṇas, and they do not respect their elders.
Because of this, they are unable to attain this dhāraṇī.
Having little merit and virtue, and being narrow and inferior in wisdom,
such sentient beings are unable to hear it.
They are unable to uphold it or generate reverence for this dhāraṇī,
which can extinguish all transgressions.
This is the secret treasury of all Tathāgatas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Great Yakṣa General Vajrapāṇi, saying:

"Good son, I now wish to go to the eastern direction, passing beyond Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of *koṭis* of *nayutas* of Ganges Rivers."
There is a world named Ratnapradīpa.
There is a great city adorned with the seven precious jewels;
that city is one yojana in width on all four sides.
The multitude of people there will be secure, prosperous,
and joyful; those men, women, boys, and girls will all be adorned with various necklaces and ornaments.
A supreme and wondrous jeweled crown appeared spontaneously;
his countenance was dignified and majestic, and he possessed great power.
Through diligence, he achieved accomplishment, and through wisdom, he attained thorough penetration.
In that city there was a king named Ratnottama,
who was attended and surrounded by eight hundred million ministers.
The king’s principal queen was named Prabhāratnā.
There were two hundred thousand palace attendants,
all like celestial maidens, who served him before and behind.
Within that world, flowers and fruits grew spontaneously.
Furthermore, all the fragrant trees are made of the seven treasures;
all the flowers that grow in water are composed of various jewels, while all the flowers that grow on land are made of pure gold.
The lifespan of the people of that country is eight million *koṭis* of years.
Having accomplished the ten wholesome actions, he developed great pure faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
That king transformed the world through the teaching of the Good Dharma, benefiting sentient beings.
In that world, there was a Buddha.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Citraratnavicitravarṇasupratiṣṭhitaviśuddha extensively performs the buddha-work in that world,
surrounded before and behind by an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and immeasurable koṭis of ṛṣis.
The body of that Tathāgata is the color of purple-gold.
He is endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs of excellence.
His halo extends one fathom, its brilliance blazing forth.
The bodies of all these bodhisattvas are the color of purple gold;
they are adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, possess unimpeded eloquence, and sit upon precious lotus pedestals,
constantly recollecting the name of the *Vast Jewel Pavilion Well-Established Secret Dhāraṇī*.
By virtue of the majestic spiritual power of that dhāraṇī,
such supreme merits are accomplished. That Buddha,
the World-Honored One, for the sake of all sentient beings...
I shall expound this dharani method.
By hearing this dharani, those sentient beings will constantly obtain peace and happiness.
They were separated from the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras;
all gates to the evil destinies were closed, and the pure path to the heavens was opened.
All those sentient beings conceived the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Abiding in great compassion, he is free from all enmity, like water and milk blended together.
In the distant past, when that Buddha-Bhagavān was practicing the bodhisattva path,
he cultivated this dharani method and made such a vow.
May all sentient beings who are born in my land all certainly attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
If there are sentient beings who hear this dhāraṇī...
One should uphold, recite, and diligently practice it,
remembering it without forsaking it, even upon merely hearing its name;
or else touching it with the hand, wearing it upon the body, or seeing it with the eyes.
Whether written on silk or plain cloth, or inscribed upon walls,
should any sentient beings behold it— whether they have committed the five heinous crimes,
the four grave offenses, or slandered the True Dharma— [they shall be purified].
They slander the noble ones; they are butchers, executioners, and slaughterers;
they are blind, deaf, sightless, and leprous;
they are mute, lepers, and those afflicted with abscesses; they are impoverished and lowly.
Those with indeterminate karma, those bound by the snares of Māra,
those fallen into wrong views, those afflicted by Vināyakas,
those harmed by malevolent stars, and those harmed by the seven luminaries.
Upon hearing the name of this dhāraṇī,
those individuals will certainly realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
or, even those who have received the bodies of animals [shall do so].
Deer, birds, mosquitoes, gadflies, moths, ants,
and various other insects born from wombs, from transformations, or from moisture—
should any of those sentient beings hear the name of this dhāraṇī, [they shall be liberated].
"You shall certainly and decisively realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, free from all doubt.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these words,
the entire great assembly was filled with immense joy, and the hairs on their bodies stood on end.
At that time, it rained *pāṭala* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, *puṇḍarīka* flowers, and *māndārava* flowers;
and in the midst of the sky, various kinds of subtle and exquisite celestial music spontaneously resounded.
At that time, every member of the great assembly perceived their own bodies radiating light.
Before the Tathāgata, seven-jeweled, wondrous banners spontaneously emerged,
exquisite, magnificent, and pleasing to behold for all people.
The banner has four pillars, four gates, and four stairways, radiating brilliant light.
On each of the four faces of the banner is a great jewel;
its light is like the sun, shining universally throughout the world.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable precious jewels strung upon the lattice,
with countless jeweled bells suspended from above,
and variegated silks and brocades fashioned into banners and canopies.
It was adorned and embellished with many exquisite flowers interspersed throughout.
At that time, the great earth shook in six ways,
manifesting the signs of quaking, roaring, trembling, surging, subsiding, and heaving.
The palaces of all the devas were bathed in this radiance;
wherever the light reached, all beings were awakened.
It was likewise so for the devas of the Four Great Kings and the ṛṣi-devas.
All the palaces of Māra were suddenly filled with radiance,
causing them all great terror; the Vināyakas, struck with fear and trembling,
fled in haste beyond the boundaries of the realm, seeking refuge and protection.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested a great white tuft of hair between his two shoulders.
Its light pervaded all worlds and all buddha-fields.
Those Tathāgatas who beheld this light—
Even as they comprehend the meaning of the dhāraṇī that was spoken,
the light, having arrived, gradually retracts of its own accord and vanishes after circling above the crown of the head of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
All the Tathāgatas of the ten directions raised their voices in unison to praise the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, saying:
"Excellent, Tathāgata Śākyamuni!"
You should now go to the world-system Jewel Lamp, to the presence of the Tathāgata Subhavyūharatnavicitravarṇasupratiṣṭhitaviśuddha,
to behold him, attend upon him, and extensively proclaim the Dharma of the Great Jewel Pavilion’s Well-Established Secret Dhāraṇī.
Why is this? Because this dhāraṇī possesses great power and great excellence, as all the Tathāgatas of the past have collectively protected and remembered it.
If anyone hears the name of this dhāraṇī or touches it with their hand, [they shall attain benefit].
That person will certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni,
having heard the voices of praise from those Tathāgatas of the ten directions, [responded].
He further emitted immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of rays of light and addressed the assembly, saying:
"I now wish to go to the world-system of Jewel Lamp."
"Come quickly, for now is the very time.
At that moment, the Tathāgata rose from his seat and approached the seven-jeweled banner, stroking it with his hand.
Thereupon, from within the banner, there suddenly emerged a sublime adamantine throne, fragrant, pure, and most excellent.
Upon this seat,
there further appeared exquisite lotus flowers variegated with the seven treasures,
with stems of gold and pedestals of red jewels.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spread his seat upon a lotus flower and sat down.
Thereupon, the entire world shook violently.
The Tathāgata then entered the Great Jewel Purification Samādhi.
Once he had entered meditative absorption, by the spiritual power of the Buddha,

he took with him the entire assembly and all the bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, along with immeasurable koṭis of vidyādharas and their retinues, Vajrapāṇi, Guhyapada, Śakra, Brahmā, and the gods of the Four Great Kings.
He ascended into the void and proceeded toward the eastern direction,
traversing immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *koṭi* buddha-fields across as many Ganges Rivers as there are sands,
all in a mere moment through the Buddha’s supernatural power.
Descending from the sky into the world-system Ratnapradīpa,
he approached that Buddha’s abode to pay his respects and inquire after his well-being,
asking whether he was free from illness and affliction, and whether his daily life was light and at ease.
Then the assembly of Śākyas presented a thousand-petaled lotus flower made of the seven precious jewels to that Buddha.
At that time, the Tathāgata, while within the profound and wondrous assembly,
extended his golden hand to comfort Śākyamuni Tathāgata, who was then moved to sit upon a jeweled banner.
He addressed the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, saying:
"You have already turned the Great Wheel of Dharma and subdued the hosts of Māra;
you have lit the great torch of the Dharma and established the banner of the Dharma."
Having struck the great Dharma drum and blown the great Dharma conch in that world,
and having performed the Buddha-work and realized what is to be realized,
he now likewise does so here in this Jambudvīpa.
He shall turn the wheel of Dharma once more and expound the treasury of all dharmas.
As soon as these words were spoken, those buddha-fields shook in eighteen ways:
namely, first, they trembled; second, they surged and boiled.
Third, like waves; fourth, shaking with sound;
fifth, roaring and crashing; sixth, awakening all sentient beings.
Within each of these movements, there are again three [aspects].
This refers to shaking, universal shaking, and so forth, up to total universal shaking.
At that time, exquisite flowers rained from the heavens as various miraculous transformations were manifested,
and natural music issued forth from the midst of space.
The great nāga kings rained down great and wondrous jewels,
various kinds of exquisite incenses, various kinds of exquisite garments,
various kinds of necklaces, and supreme, wonderful red gems.
Shell, pearl, and the great wondrous jewel of Vairocana;
the sun-treasury pearl and the moon-treasury pearl;
the sun-light pearl and the moon-light pearl; and the auspicious-treasury pearl.
They rained down various *padma* flowers, *kumuda* flowers,
*puṇḍarīka* flowers, *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers,
golden flowers, and silver flowers.
A profusion of exquisite pearl necklaces fell down.
At that time, the devas in the midst of the void raised voices of joy and praised the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, saying:
Excellent, Śākyamuni Tathāgata! Excellent, Śākyamuni Tathāgata!
You wish to turn the wheel of the Dharma once again at this time.
He erected the great, wondrous jewel, the Dharma-banner of the wish-fulfilling gem, in the midst of Jambudvīpa— namely,
the Mahāratnavipula-ratnakūṭa-guhya-susthitadhāraṇī, the Great King of Spells.
He caused it to spread widely throughout the world.
At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Viśvarūpa-viśuddha-susthita-ratna emitted various rays of light from the great white tuft of hair between his two eyebrows.
That light reached universally all Buddha-lands throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
When those Buddhas beheld this light,
they all realized and knew that he was about to expound the meaning of this dhāraṇī.
That light further reached the trichiliocosm,
as well as the palaces of the devas, the palaces of the nāgas, all the hells, the animal realm, the realm of Yama, and the hosts of asuras.
All beings were universally bathed in this light;
they knew that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was about to preach the Dharma.
Once the light had pervaded everywhere, it gradually withdrew and was reabsorbed.
Circling around the crown of the Buddha’s head, he suddenly vanished. At that time,
throughout the worlds of the ten directions, all Buddhas— as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers—
each manifested great spiritual transformations within their respective lands together with their retinues.
In the midst of the void, he manifested seven precious, wondrous banners.
Within each banner, he fashioned a lion throne made of Jambūnada gold.
Then, the various Buddhas each sat upon their respective thrones and together arrived at the assembly.
At that time, the Tathāgata Viśvarūpaviśuddharatna saw the Buddhas of the ten directions arrive at the assembly and exchanged greetings with those Buddhas.
He further made offerings to that Buddha with various kinds of supernatural transformations.
Having completed his offerings, he returned to his original seat.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva in this assembly named Ratnagarbha.
Rising from his seat, he approached the Tathāgata Viśvarūpa-viśuddha-supratiṣṭhita-ratna,
joined his palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One, in this assembly today, there are the Buddhas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas.”
Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, celestial rishis, and luminous rishis,
with the Vajradhara Bodhisattva as their leader.
Once the assembly had gathered, through immeasurable miraculous transformations,
[the Bodhisattva] made this request: "I pray that the World-Honored One will,
for the sake of this great multitude, expound the Dharma of the Great Treasure Pavilion Secret Well-Established Dhāraṇī."
Thus, having been earnestly entreated three times by the assembly for the World-Honored One to preach the Dharma,
at that time the Tathāgata Viśvarūpaviśuddhasupratiṣṭhita-ratna addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnagarbha, saying:
"You should now go to the place of Śākyamuni Buddha; he shall explain it for you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnagarbha immediately went to the place of Śākyamuni Buddha.
With palms joined, he prostrated, circumambulated him three times to the right,
and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I now entreat the Tathāgata to act for the sake of this great assembly."
He expounded the Dharma of the Vast, Precious, Secret, Well-Established,
and Pure Dhāraṇī for the sake of bringing benefit to all sentient beings.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha...
Having seen that the Bodhisattva Ratnagarbha had made his request,
he addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Good son, you should now take up the vajra."
In the midst of the great assembly, he struck the ground.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi,
in accordance with the Buddha’s command, took up the vajra.
In the midst of the great assembly, he struck the earth with his hand.
At that moment, the great earth split open in response to the sound, forming four-cornered fissures;
the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
At that moment, from the sunken ground, there suddenly emerged a multi-storied pavilion made of the seven treasures.
Its four corners, four pillars, and four gates were magnificent and extraordinary,
with perfect and complete features and a brilliant, blazing radiance.
There are four stairways, three yojanas high,
with a length and breadth each measuring exactly five yojanas.
Within these banners is a subtle and exquisite stupa made of Jambū-river gold.
It was adorned with immeasurable precious jewels and covered above by a net of the seven treasures.
Immeasurable jeweled bells hung from its four corners,
interspersed with exquisite flowers and silken streamers.
Within that wondrous stūpa are the entire bodily relics of three Tathāgatas.
At that time, all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the ten directions together made offerings to the relics within the stūpa.
The various bodhisattvas likewise made offerings, paid respect, and offered praise;
they scattered flowers, burned incense, and applied perfumes and powdered incense;
they hung silk streamers, banners, and canopies, and performed various kinds of music.
At that time, the assembly of all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, garuḍas, humans,
non-humans, and others, all gazed upon this marvelous and unprecedented wonder.
They asked, "From where has this precious stūpa come?
and they praised it with loud voices, exclaiming, "How marvelous! How rare!
They circumambulated and sang hymns of praise to the banner and the precious stūpa.
Having completed the circumambulation, they joined their palms and prostrated with their heads at his feet.
At that moment, a subtle and wondrous sound issued from within the banner, proclaiming:
"O great assembly, you should look into the sky."
When the assembly heard this sound,
they all gazed into the air and again beheld a great cloud of lapis lazuli at the edge of the sky;
within that precious cloud, there were characters formed of gold.
Having written down this Secret Dharani of the Good Abiding in the Vast Jewel Pavilion,
a voice resounded again from the midst of space, saying:
"All of you should read this dharani mantra."
After these words were spoken,
before each of the Buddhas who had come from the ten directions— numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges— a cloud of lapis lazuli jewels appeared.
Upon it, this dhāraṇī mantra was inscribed with letters of gold.
Again, such a voice issued forth, saying:
"Homage to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni!
You may now open the door of that śarīra-stūpa."
Within that jeweled stūpa are the entire-body relics of three Tathāgatas.
Due to the manifestation of great supernatural transformations and sublime signs by those relics,
those entire-body Tathāgatas appear within this assembly.
I shall now fully explain this dhāraṇī mantra along with the vidyā-dharmas for the accomplishment of the maṇḍala.
At that time, all the Buddhas who had come from the ten directions spoke these words in unison:
I only pray that Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha,
will open the door of that stūpa for the great assembly,
so that all sentient beings may behold the complete body of the Tathāgata and obtain great benefit.
These are the Tathāgata Ratnapuṣpapativyūhaketu,
the Tathāgata Suvajraratnottararāja, and the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaviśuddhaprabha.
At that time, Śākyamuni—
Immediately, by means of his supernatural power, he went before the jeweled stupa;
extending his golden hand, adorned with the marks of a hundred blessings, he opened the door of that stupa with his right hand and revealed the entire body-relics of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Tathāgata of Complete Body within the precious stūpa again praised Śākyamuni Tathāgata, saying:
"Excellent, Śākyamuni Tathāgata!"
"Now, within Jambudvīpa, you shall turn the Wheel of Dharma once more.
You may ascend the lion throne within this stūpa.
At that time, Śākyamuni Tathāgata immediately ascended into the stūpa.
He sat upon the same seat as all the Tathāgatas with their bodies intact.
At that time, within the assembly, there was the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi,
who prostrated himself before the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
With palms joined in reverence, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, from where do these Tathāgatas within this stūpa come? From whence have they arrived?"
The Buddha said, "Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
In the distant past, incalculable, immeasurable, and countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago,
this Jambudvīpa was filled with many people who lived in peace, security, abundance, and joy."
The five grains ripen naturally without being sown;
people have no sense of "self" or "other," nor do they engage in hoarding.
At this time, even the name of "Buddha" does not exist.
There was a great mountain named King of Jewel Mountains.
Within that Jewel Mountain dwelt three rishis:
the first was named Ratnaśikhin, the second Suvarṇaśikhin, and the third Vajraśikhin.
Those three sages focused their minds with single-minded devotion on the Triple Gem— the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Saṅgha— and further thought:
"When shall we realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?"
"To deliver all sentient beings. Having formed this thought,
that assembly of sages remained silent for a moment,
then again gave rise to the previous thought.
By virtue of this reflection, he immediately realized the samādhi of the various pavilions for all sentient beings— namely, loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy—
and attained the divine eye, whereby he beheld the Heaven of Pure Abodes above.
Again, a voice spoke from the air, saying:
"Excellent, noble being! Excellent, noble being!
You are able to give rise to the supreme vow and seek great, perfect enlightenment."
Have you not heard?
There is a sublime and wondrous Dharma called the *Mahāratnakuṭa-guhya-supratiṣṭhita-dhāraṇī*,
which was previously expounded by the Tathāgatas of old.
This is well done for the benefit of all sentient beings.
All who hear it will certainly not regress from unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
and all Buddha-dharmas shall swiftly manifest before them.
All samādhis shall likewise manifest before them;
all dhāraṇī dharma-gates shall likewise manifest before them;
and they shall be able to thoroughly subdue all demonic armies.
The great torch of the Dharma shall be ignited, and all seeds of goodness shall become manifest.
One shall achieve the six pāramitās.
[This shall extend to] all those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, Yama’s world, and the asura hosts.
All who hear this mantra shall attain liberation;
they will forever transcend birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
In a future age, within this Jambudvīpa, [they shall likewise be so].
There are sentient beings who are unfilial toward their parents;
those who do not revere śramaṇas, do not revere brahmins, or do not revere the elders;
those who slander the true Dharma and slander the noble ones—beings who ought to fall into hell.

If there is a woman who desires to obtain a son,

If there are people who recite and maintain other mantras that have no efficacy, [this one shall succeed].
If one bathes with this water, results will be attained immediately.
In this way, all things will be swiftly accomplished,
and other undertakings as well shall be successful.
Chapter Five: The Method for Reciting the Anuprāsa-mantra. Regarding the method for reciting the Anuprāsa-mantra:
if one recites it ten thousand times, all obstructing spirits and demons will [be subdued].
They all came to pay homage at the feet of the mantra-holder and spoke these words:
"Protect us; do not take our lives."
Those whom one commissions will certainly achieve their purpose.
If one recites it twenty-one thousand times,
one will immediately cause all devas and nāgas to become lords among the gods.
All the devas shall carry out whatever words are spoken.

If recited thirty thousand times, all yakṣas and rākṣasas will be completely subdued and compliant; [the Sanskrit original lacks the mention of forty thousand times]; if recited fifty thousand times, one will be able to summon and control whatever is desired.
Whether they be devas, nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, asuras, mahoragas, as well as ṛṣis, celestial maidens,
śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, or various other persons.
If one burns agalloch incense and white mustard seeds while reciting [the mantra] sixty thousand times, one will attain the stainless samādhi.
If one recites it seventy thousand times, one will become a rishi-cakravartin king.
If one recites it eighty thousand times, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and his retinue will appear before one.
If one recites it ninety thousand times, one will receive the gift of fearlessness from all the bodhisattvas.
If one recites it one hundred thousand times, one will see all past Tathāgatas in their entirety;
one’s movements will be unimpeded according to one’s wishes,
and one will obtain all dhāraṇīs, sūtras, and śāstras, as well as the empowerment of all Tathāgatas.
It causes one to realize unsurpassed bodhi,
and all various supramundane dharmas to be fully accomplished;
there are no Buddhas, Tathāgatas, who do not rejoice therein.
Chapter Six: Miscellaneous Mantras. Before sitting before the altar, one should recite this mantra:
Oṃ maṇi-kuṇḍali hūṃ hūṃ svāhā. Recite it seven times, and then sit.
Perform the remaining methods of protection.
Next, the mantra for binding the boundary (*sīmābandha*) is as follows:
*Oṃ maṇivijaye dharadhara hūṃ hūṃ svāhā*. Recite this mantra seven times over white mustard seeds.
Scattering [the substances] within the altar constitutes the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*).
Next, the mantra for binding the boundaries of the ten directions is as follows:
*Oṃ nivārita-maṇi-ālojira-kīrti hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. Recite this mantra over the perfumed water.
Recite the mantra over white mustard seeds one hundred and eight times and scatter them in the ten directions.
To ward off Vināyakas, recite the following mantra:
Oṃ maṇi-prabhavani hana hana hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Recite this mantra twenty-one times over ashes and water.
[The mantras] are scattered throughout the ten directions.
The *uṣṇīṣa-mantra* is as follows:
Oṃ vajramani tiṣṭha tiṣṭha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ. Recite this mantra seven times; with the hand consecrated by the mantra, rub one’s own head.
The mantra for protecting the robe is:
Oṃ maṇivipulakṣīri hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this mantra over scented water and sprinkle it upon the robe.
The mantra for washing the hands is:
Oṃ vaṭe vaṭe mahāmane hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this mantra over water;
use it to wash the hands and sprinkle it all over the body.
The mantra for bathing is as follows:
Oṃ sunir-malāvadhi hara hara pāpmanī hūṃ svāhā. Recite this mantra one hundred and eight times over white mustard seeds mixed with water, and bathe the body.
Next, the mantra for binding the protection is as follows:
Oṃ maṇidāri hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this mantra to bind the protection of all incense, flowers, fruits, and other articles used.
All [of these] are to be bound and protected by means of this mantra.
The mantra for binding the cord is:
Oṃ dṛdhe dṛdhe vimālakari hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. Next, the mantra for scattering flowers is:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatapuṣpamālini hūṃ hūṃ. Recite this mantra over all incense and flowers and scatter them;
recite it also at the time of scattering.
The mantra for scented ointment is as follows:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatagandhamani-spharaṇa hūṃ hūṃ. Recite this mantra to consecrate the incense and smear it upon the altar.
The mantra for burning incense is as follows:
Oṃ śāvari-da-maṇi-ābhrakūṭa-spharaṇa-vigati hūṃ. The mantra for lighting the lamps is:
Oṃ śāvari-sikharī-dhavalī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. The mantra for offering to all the devas, ghosts, and others outside the maṇḍala is:
Oṃ pravaragotra-vati sara sara hūṃ hūṃ. Next is the Aṅka mantra;
one should also scatter parched rice and flower-powder daily before the deity.
Recite this mantra while scattering [the offerings].
The mantra is:
Oṃ mahāmanibhūṣāya dara dara hūṃ hūṃ. Next, on the central altar, offer food to the Buddha every day and recite this mantra:
Oṃ mahāmantrī-vajri hūṃ hūṃ vara vara hūṃ hūṃ. Next, the mantra for offering the fire-oblation (homa) is:
Oṃ śvāra sapraga gagana pradarani hūṃ hūṃ. Next, the mantra for holding the rosary is:
Oṃ aluñjira mani-pravartaya hūṃ. Having recited this mantra seven times, one immediately accomplishes all the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of mantra-rites of the Tathāgatas.
If one follows the model for delineating the altar boundaries,
one should recite this mantra over the cord seven times and use it to mark out the boundary lines.
Next, perform the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*) and recite the mantra:

*Oṃ vajramanikara kiṃkiri kiri hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. This mantra is for the purpose of binding the full lotus posture; it should be understood that the preceding mantra is for the occasion when one is about to recite [the main mantra].
Next, at the time of recitation, the mantra is:
Oṃ subhara vartita vege mani mani svāhā. This is the mantra for announcing to all Buddhas, praying that they may take cognizance: [Mantra follows].
Oṃ sarvatathāgatānāṃ vyūhasiddhārthāya hūṃ hūṃ maṇikanaṃ svāhā. Next, the mantra for inviting all the Buddhas is as follows:
Oṃ suvīra-praprapāre dūru dūru hūṃ hūṃ. Next, the mantra for requesting the fulfillment of wishes is:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatādhiṣṭhita-citta-saṃlakṣya-vajri hūṃ hūṃ. When reciting this mantra, one should form this thought:
May all Buddhas protect with equanimity and bestow the power of firm resolve.
Next, seek the Bodhisattva’s vow-mantra, which is:
Oṃ sumitrabodhanī hana hana hūṃ. While reciting this mantra, one should form this thought:
May I obtain the wondrous, vast, and extensive treasury that radiates the light of fearlessness.
I entreat all devas and nāgas with this mantra:
Oṃ abhisamaye bhaṣṭri dara dara hūṃ. One should form this thought.
The infinite samaya-vajra is held and is immovable and indestructible.
Next, the mantra for inviting the Four Heavenly Kings and others is:
Oṃ maṇivika-bodhe hūṃ. The mantra for the attendant is: [Oṃ maṇivika-bodhe hūṃ].
Oṃ śivamāni hulu hulu hūṃ. Recite this mantra to perform the protective binding for the ritual attendants outside the maṇḍala.
The mantra for entering the maṇḍala is:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatavajriṇi dara dara hūṃ hūṃ. At that time, one should kneel on the ground beside the maṇḍala with palms joined.
Having recited this mantra, one should form this thought:
"May all Tathāgatas empower me with vajra-power.
Next, offer to all Buddhas, all Bodhisattvas, and the various devas with the following mantra:
Oṃ vīra vīra ceka gagana vāsini ra hu ra hu hūṃ. All incense, flowers, food, and drink should be offered while reciting this mantra.
Next, the mantra for protecting the body is:
Oṃ maṇi svabhāve vigatabhaye arakṣata maṇi hūṃ. Next, the mantra for dispatching the holy ones is:
Oṃ sarvatathāgata-kurundi-samara-vigati-śvala-śvala hūṃ svāhā. This mantra is to be used universally in all places.
This refers to offering superior *argha*, incense, flowers, food, drink, and so forth.
All of these are heart-mantras (*hṛdaya-mantra*),
each possessing extraordinary and sublime power.
If one intends to employ this, one should first recite it eight hundred times,
and only then perform the ritual procedure.
Merely by reciting it, all virtuous deeds will be accomplished.
All evil karma is extinguished;
one is completely liberated from all suffering and affliction;
and the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, bestow upon one the definitive prophecy of enlightenment.
When one attains Buddhahood,
all evil karma from previous lives shall be completely dissolved by upholding this mantra,
and one will swiftly realize Bodhi.
One shall obtain immeasurable merits equal to those of immeasurable Ganges-sands;
one shall swiftly attain perfect enlightenment and be able to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Chapter Seven: The Ritual for Establishing the Mandala. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke the ritual for establishing the mandala.
First, select an auspicious site and then construct the altar.
The altar ground should have four gates and be painted with five colors.
Mix the pigments with fragrant water in a new vessel,
and then use them.
In the center of the altar, construct a small altar.
It shall be two cubits square,
adorned with white sandalwood and saffron;
its great altar shall be four cubits.
Adorn it by smearing it with cow dung.
Within the small altar, paint an image of a Buddha.
Before that Buddha, fashion a lotus flower.
Adorned with the seven precious jewels,
one should paint a wheel within the center of the lotus pedestal;
the wheel has a hundred spokes.
It has a felloe and a rim, with the wheel adorned in gold;
outside the wheel, flaming light is painted.
The stalk of the lotus flower is the color of lapis lazuli.

On the left, paint the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, displaying a wrathful gesture and holding a white fly-whisk in his hand; according to one version, he holds a vajra in his left hand and a battle-axe in his right. On the right, paint the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabhāvajra.
Adorned with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments,
one hand holds a precious jewel and the other hand grasps a white fly-whisk (according to another version, he holds a rosary). At each of the four corners, the Four Great Heavenly Kings are depicted.
His body is clad in armor and his hands hold weapons;
he is adorned with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments,
and assumes an expression of wrathful anger.
Within that small altar, one should paint steps and paths made of the seven treasures.
Above the altar, hang silk banners and canopies.
The main gate of the altar opens toward the east.
At each of the four corners, place a golden or silver flask;
if no golden flask is available,
use an earthenware flask coated with gold.
Fill the center with scented water and place exquisite flowers within;
if there is no silver vase, [use another].
One should likewise fill [the vessels] with milk in this manner.
Inside the eastern gate of the small altar, on the southern side,
one should paint the goddess Śrī.
Adorned with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments,
one should paint the goddess Śaṅkhinī on the northern side.
At the center of the mandala gate, one should paint the form of the Vajradūtī goddess.
He has eight arms,
adorned with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments,
and holds swords and staves in his hands.
On the small altar, hang various banners and canopies;
light thirty-two lamps;
and scatter various flowers and fruits upon the altar.
Before the image of the Buddha,
place an incense burner and burn *sugandha* (sahagandha) incense;
outside the small altar, [perform the following].
Place a silver incense burner and burn agallochum incense before the Maṇi Yakṣa;
burn storax incense before the Four Great Kings— namely, frankincense, *sajjarasa*, and resinous olibanum— and burn white sandalwood incense before the goddess Śrī.

One should burn agalloch incense before the goddess Śaṅkhinī and sāragga incense—resin from the *sāra* tree—before the Vajradūtī; furthermore, one should offer various foods and drinks to each of these deities individually.
Outside each of the four gates of the small mandala, one should erect auspicious banners.
Outside the eastern gate, one should paint the goddess Haritī,
surrounded by her seven ghost-children.
Outside the southern gate, paint the deity Maheśvara;
outside the western gate, paint the rākṣasī Puṣpadantī;
and outside the northern gate, paint the goddess Bhīmā.
Seven court ladies surround him.
Along the four sides of the altar, thirty-two arrows are inserted;
each arrow is individually painted with five-colored silk streamers suspended from it and wrapped around it.
Hang five-colored banners on the four sides of the altar.
One should prepare seven kinds of oil cakes.
Outside the main altar, further place thirty-two basins of pure water.
Place various kinds of flowers in the basin.
Set out thirty-two water-pots for purification;
within each pot, place a different kind of gruel.
There were thirty-two incense burners,
one hundred and eight lamps were lit,
and one hundred and eight garlands of *rūṣaka* flowers were suspended; various powdered incenses were scattered and various types of incense were burned.
That which is called guggulu,
frankincense, sarjarasa,
and *mūrvā*— namely, the sweet clover— and sandalwood.
Agallochum (*śrīkhaṇḍa*):
a medicinal substance derived from *tagara*. Balsam (*suhaka*):
a blue resin (*sāragandha*). The five-flavored incense (*pañcarasagandha*).
Camphor, musk, and saffron.
Using fragrances such as red sandalwood as unguents,
one should apply them upon the deities.
Furthermore, milk, curd, granulated sugar, rock honey, and water were each placed in eight jars.

Additionally, there were eight basins each containing milk porridge—made by mixing husked rice, mung beans, sesame, and cow butter—and "joy-balls" (*modaka*), which were made from husked rice mixed with a small amount of sugar and wheat flour, combined with honey syrup.
Furthermore, he filled four earthen bowls with oil, four earthen bowls with ghee,
four earthen bowls with granulated sugar,
and four earthen bowls with sesame seeds.
Four earthenware bowls of fruit and four earthenware bowls of the seven kinds of grains;
having prepared these various foods, scatter them outside the altar.
These are what are called *māṣapūpa*,
fried cakes,
small-bean fried cakes— namely, those made from mung bean flour mixed with grape juice— and sesame fried cakes.
Aśoka-flavored exquisite cakes,
ghee cakes,
and sugar cakes.
Furthermore, outside the western gate of the great maṇḍala,
place two fragrant water jars,
as well as the food and drink to be offered.
When about to enter the maṇḍala, first recite this mantra over the incense water jars on both sides of the gate.
The mantra is:
Oṃ mahā-vipula pratisarati-ścitte svasti abhiṣiñca mā hūṃ sarva-tathāgata-niṣyanda vāra vāra saṃvara saṃvara hūṃ hūṃ. With this mantra, empower the consecration jar water.
Those who recite this mantra can eliminate all evil karma from previous lifetimes and cause both body and mind to attain purity.
All Buddhas come to protect,
sustain, and bestow upon them the prediction of enlightenment,
granting them fearlessness for all their activities.
It enables one to achieve entry into the Tathāgata’s samādhi,
realize the profound Dharma, and,
through the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), ascend to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to attain perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Chapter Eight: On Painted Images. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:
"I shall now explain the method for painting images, by which one can accomplish all undertakings."
One should take new white cotton cloth that has not yet had its threads cut,
measuring one cubit, two cubits, three cubits, four cubits,
or even up to seven cubits, making it equal on all four sides.
Paint one Tathāgata seated upon a lion throne in the posture of preaching the Dharma;
to the right of the image, paint the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.
He is red, white, and crimson in color;
he has twelve arms, all of which hold swords and staves,
and he has four faces.
The face directly in front is upright and joyful;
the face on the left side displays an expression of wrath;
and the face on the right side has fangs protruding upward.
Furthermore, one side of his face has a terrifying expression with knitted brows,
and his two eyes are angry;
he is adorned and embellished with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments.
He sits upon a lotus pedestal in the *ardhaparyaṅka* posture.
To the left of the Tathāgata, one should paint the Bodhisattva Maṇivajra,
who has four faces, the front of which is joyful.
The right face is blue in color,
having the appearance of the deity Mahākāla;
the left face is reddish-brown in color.
The upper half has the face of a lion and the lower half the face of a human;
the rear face displays an expression of wrath,
with furrowed brows and bared teeth, and is light green in color.
He has sixteen arms;
his right hands hold wish-fulfilling jewels in the gesture of offering to the Buddha,
and his left hands hold lotus flowers.
With one hand, bestow fearlessness by extending the five fingers upward as if slightly lowered;
with both hands, join them in *añjali*.
The remaining hands all grasp various implements and weapons, namely:
a three-pointed spear, a wheel, a sword, a vajra, a flower casket, a rosary, a water jar, a sharp blade, a scripture case, a jeweled stupa, and Mount Sumeru.
He sits in the half-lotus posture upon the center of a lotus pedestal;
beneath his seat is the goddess Śaṅkhinī.
He has eight arms and is depicted in the posture of kneeling with palms joined in homage to the Buddha.
He sits beneath the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.
She is depicted as the goddess Śrī,
kneeling on her right knee and holding various jeweled vessels,
in the act of making offerings to the likeness of the Tathāgata.
Behind the goddess Śrī,
one should paint the messenger goddess with a smiling face.
He has four arms,
adorned with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments,
and holds a sword and a staff in his hands.
After the messenger had presented the offerings to the goddess Aparājitā,
he painted the rākṣasī Puṣpadantī,
dressed in white garments.
Holding flowers in their hands, they gaze up at the Tathāgata.
Before the great image, one should paint a lotus flower made of the seven treasures,
which has a thousand petals.
Its stem is made of lapis lazuli;
upon it is fashioned a thousand-spoked wheel with a rim,
its four sides all radiant with brilliant light.
Below that, one should paint the Four Heavenly Kings,
adorned in various ways and holding swords and staves in their hands;
beneath the seven-jeweled lotuses, one should depict a pool of the seven treasures.
Upon the banks of the pond, he fashioned many sages,
all kneeling with their right knees on the ground;
some held flowers, and others held jewels.
Some held incense burners in their hands, while others held prayer beads;
each, adorned and holding their respective offerings, gazed upon the Tathāgata and made offerings from atop the great statue.
Paint Brahmā, Śakra, and Maheśvara,
scattering flowers as an offering;
do not mix animal hide glue with the pigments.
Those who paint this image should observe the eightfold precepts of the fast.
Those who recite the mantra should wear new,
clean clothes and consume the three white foods.
On the eighth day of the month,
recite and chant before the Tathāgata according to the Dharma;
continue until the fifteenth day, completing one hundred million recitations in total.
Then, seeing one's own body emitting light,
one awakens to the unobstructed eye of wisdom and realizes the pure maṇi-samādhi.
One shall attain the rank of a wheel-turning monarch among the sages and personally behold all Tathāgatas;
if one recites this even once, one shall not fall into any of the evil realms.
Free from all greed, hatred, and delusion, and devoid of envy,
one accomplishes all merits and gathers all roots of goodness.
It is that which is protected and remembered by all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas;
it constantly comes to offer consolation and is able to encompass all the devas.
All devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans,
and others shall all come to make offerings;
kings and ministers should always pay them respect.
They shall wander fearlessly among human beings,
swiftly accomplishing all the pāramitās.
This applies even to those who merely uphold, receive, read, and recite it.
Immeasurable merit. If one can,
according to the Dharma, construct a maṇḍala, paint an image, and prepare all the requirements for the maṇḍala rites,
that person’s merit will be no different from that of a Buddha.
They shall be venerated and supported by all humans and devas;
and all Buddhas and Tathāgatas shall bestow upon this person the prediction that they will certainly realize unsurpassed bodhi.
They shall no longer receive a body from a womb;
wherever they are born, it shall always be within a lotus flower,
and they shall always be in the presence of the Buddha.
He sat together with the bodhisattvas in one place.
Chapter Nine: On Homa. At that time, the Tathāgata again expounded the homa ritual for the great assembly.
First, one must purify body and mind and cultivate pure brahmacarya;
only then should one perform the ritual procedures so that each and every dharma may be swiftly accomplished.
Generating the vast mind that benefits all sentient beings, one performs the homa offering by burning the mantra-food.
Recite this mantra:
Oṃ sarvāpatti-jalopapoha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. While reciting this mantra:
One should take sesame seeds, white mustard seeds, and clarified butter;
reciting the mantra once for each, burn them until eight thousand repetitions are completed and cast them [into the fire].
This will cause all dhāraṇī methods to be swiftly accomplished.
It subdues all obstructing spirits and deities;
all evil ghosts, those of evil karma, wicked associates,
and enemies are all brought under control.
All evil dreams, calamities, portents, and inauspicious events will naturally dissipate.
[One should prepare] *agaru* incense,
white mustard seeds, and clarified butter.
Recite the mantra once and cast it into the fire;
burn it thus for a full eight thousand times.
Any ghosts or spirits who wish to come and cause harm [will be unable to do so].
The head will split open of its own accord,
and all illnesses will be swiftly cured.
Furthermore, one should recite the mantra while mixing white mustard seeds with clarified butter (*sarpis*).
Recite the mantra once for each incense offering, completing eight thousand repetitions.
One will then attain a dwelling place free from all enemies and adversaries.
If one uses celestial wood, pine wood, and the like, mixed with clarified butter (ghṛta), [the same result is achieved].
Recite the mantra once and cast it into the fire; after doing this eight thousand times,
one will attain the abode of the Yakṣarāja and all that one desires will be accomplished.
If one takes the incense of the *śāla* tree and pine needles, mixes them with clarified butter and white mustard seeds,
and burns them upon a mountain peak while reciting the mantra for the prescribed number of times as before.
The gates of the asuras will open spontaneously,
and this person shall become a King of the Vidyādharas.
If one uses *gandhārī* wood— that is, *aṃśumatī* wood— or the filaments of *nāgapuṣpa* mixed with white mustard oil, [one may perform the rite].
If one recites the mantra once and burns [the substance] once by the side of a dragon pond for a full eight thousand times,
one will be able to subjugate all dragons;
this must be performed until they are all brought under control.
Rain falls exactly when required,
and there are no further hardships such as thunder or hail.
This is because of the various grains and the pure vegetarian food offered to the Buddha.
If one recites the name and chants the mantra for the sake of oneself or others,
burning [the substance] once for each incantation until eight thousand repetitions are complete, it will cause the five grains to ripen in abundance; if one uses white salt and chants the mantra,
burning it once for each incantation until eight thousand repetitions are complete, the same result follows.
All the yakṣiṇīs came and prostrated at his feet, saying, "Do not harm our lives;
we shall serve you as you command.
[He then prepared] rice mixed with husks and blended with ghee.
Recite the mantra once for each incense offering, completing eight thousand repetitions;
one will attain great wealth and nobility.
[To do so], take black pepper and face the sun.
When the sun is in the east, recite the mantra eight thousand times;
for each recitation, burn one [incense stick].
That person will always receive the protection of the devas and constantly receive their benefit.
If one burns sesame seeds mixed with white mustard seeds before the goddess Śrī,
one will obtain great wealth and treasures.
If one takes *ekaja* wood— meaning the wood of the *duzhong* tree— and cuts it into pieces one foot long,
reciting the mantra once for each piece and burning them until eight hundred repetitions are complete,
one shall obtain the presence of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
It is known that this person is free from all karmic obstructions and has fully realized and mastered all mundane and supramundane vidyā-mantras.
Free from all diseases,
they attain supreme victory over all enemies;
the afflictions of the world cannot defile or attach to them.
By the power of this vidyā-mantra,
all virtuous deeds shall be accomplished,
and all evil dreams and inauspicious events shall be averted.
All shall be dispersed and dissolved.
All malevolent spirits, demonic influences, and calamities resulting from improper prayers shall not attach themselves to one's person.
They shall not fall into wrong views or the various evil realms.
At that time, the Buddha told the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi: "This Dharma of the King of Dhāraṇīs possesses great majestic power."
This is the heart of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas;
it is the mother of all Buddhas;
it is that by which all Tathāgatas turn the great wheel of Dharma.
These Tathāgatas have entered the path to enlightenment;
these Tathāgatas are the torch of the Dharma of wisdom;
these Tathāgatas sound the great Dharma conch.
These Tathāgatas sit upon the vajra-seat;
these Tathāgatas have subdued the armies of Māra;
these Tathāgatas possess the most supreme secret.
It can eliminate all the afflictions of the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa;
it can exhaust the karma of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals among the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa;
and it can remove the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, pain, and distress for the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa.

The Buddha said: "First, one should use the thumbs of both hands."
Twist each ring finger;
then, hook the two middle fingers together and support the two index fingers against one another.
Spread the two little fingers apart.
Raise the right elbow and let the left elbow hang downward;
with eyes glaring in a wrathful expression, the mouth tightly bites the lower lip while the gaze is fixed upon the left elbow.

The Buddha said: "It should be as before, with only the two hands spread apart;
the two index fingers must not touch each other.
Furthermore, change the posture to the full lotus position (paryaṅka)."
Placing the mudrā at the heart, generate great compassion.
Gaze with pure eyes and recite the mantra with single-minded concentration.
Then, he spoke the mantra:
Oṃ dhuru dhuru maṇi maṇi mahāmaṇi guhyamaṇi svāhā. For one who performs this mudrā-rite, virtuous words shall issue from their mouth and all their aspirations shall be fulfilled.
When one contemplates this, the Bodhisattva Ratnavajra is filled with great joy;
he protects and mindfuly regards the mantra-practitioner as a mother cares for her child,
and all that is sought shall be attained.
Next, the method for the mudrā and mantra of the Four Heavenly Kings is explained.
The Buddha said: "One should place the right hand on the hip and raise the index finger."
Press the little finger of the left hand against the thumb,
extend the remaining three fingers vertically, and place them upon the navel.
The practitioner of the mantra should maintain a mind of loving-kindness.
Manifesting an expression of wrath and staring with fixed eyes, he recites this mantra:
*Oṃ rukāparidītya jaḥ jaḥ hūṃ*. By forming this mudrā and reciting this mantra, one invokes the Four Heavenly Kings.
One will immediately obtain the most excellent protection that arrives swiftly.
Next, the method for the mudrā and mantra of the goddess Śrī is explained.
The Buddha said: "First, one should extend both arms."
Then, join the two palms together so they touch,
place the two thumbs side by side with a distance of one cun between them,
and slightly curve them as if feigning.
The two index fingers are curved like hooks;
the remaining three fingers on each hand are paired and extended toward one another, forming the shape of a lotus flower.
Having performed this, one recites the mantra:
Oṃ vimalevara-vati svabhāra hūṃ. When this rite is performed, all that the heart desires shall be attained according to one's wish.
Next, the method for the mudrā and mantra of the goddess Śaṅkhinī is explained.
The Buddha said: "One should raise the right hand near the left breast and form a slight fist;
then extend the index finger."
Covering his left hand and placing it upon his left knee,
he bends his body forward and stares with fixed eyes,
reciting this mantra:
Oṃ ḍākinīni ve sara hūṃ. When this rite is performed,
the goddess Ḍākinī will swiftly come to provide protection for the practitioner.
Whatever one performs according to one's will shall all be accomplished.
Next, the Buddha spoke of the mudrā and mantra method for the Vajradūtī goddess:
"One should bend the left arm so that the elbow and shoulder point upward and are thrust slightly forward."
Cover both breasts with the palms held askew;
then, bend the right hand over to cover the left hand.
Lower the elbows downward and extend the neck forward.
Slightly bending his body, he recites this mantra:
Oṃ akṣaṇi tathāgatam añcaṭaṭa hasini hūṃ. By performing this rite, he invites the Vajradūta goddess.
Rejoicing, they shall quickly come to abide where the mantra-practitioner is;
one may perform rites at will, and all shall be accomplished.
Next, the methods for the mudrās and mantras for requesting the various deities to abide within the maṇḍala are explained.
The Buddha said: "One should use both hands with the ten fingers interlaced and turned inward to cover the navel,
while standing on the ground."
He stands with his right foot pointing straight down, planted firmly on the ground,
while his left foot is extended horizontally to the left,
planted like the character "T" (ding) in the world.
Recite this mantra:
Oṃ samantakāra paripūrani dhaka dhaka hūṃ phaṭ. When performing this rite:
All those deities gathered like clouds from every direction,
fulfilling all prayers and aspirations with steadfast protection and mindfulness;
thus, the practitioner shall swiftly attain accomplishment.
Next, the method for the mudrā and mantra of the goddess Padmadantī is explained.
The Buddha said: "One should join the palms of both hands and slightly bend the ten fingers so that they resemble the form of a lotus."
Lift the mudrā and place it upon the left shoulder;
then, gradually lower the mudrā until it rests near the left side of the heart.
Recite this mantra:

regarding him with eyes of loving-kindness,
along with the Vajradhara Bodhisattvas, the Four Heavenly Kings, and others.

one should constantly read, recite, receive, uphold, copy,
